question:
Based on the chest X-ray findings, which combination of radiographic signs is most suggestive of a pulmonary embolism in this patient?

A) Wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity in the right lower lung field and engorgement of the right descending pulmonary artery
B) Wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity in the left lower lung field and engorgement of the left descending pulmonary artery
C) Engorgement of the right descending pulmonary artery and a focal peripheral hyperlucency in the right lung field
D) Wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity in the right lower lung field and a focal peripheral hyperlucency in the left lung field
E) Engorgement of the left descending pulmonary artery and a focal peripheral hyperlucency in the left lung field
F) Engorgement of the right descending pulmonary artery and a wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity in the left lower lung field

observations.value: indicated by white arrow in figure_1b
indicated by white arrow in figure_1b
indicated by blue arrow in figure_1b
Right side (per expert analysis)

missing_evidence: direct visual confirmation of wedge-shaped opacity morphology in right lower lung
direct measurement/visual confirmation of right descending pulmonary artery engorgement

gate.reason: Tool p0:tool:2 identifies Hampton's hump (blue arrow), Fleischner sign (white arrow), and Westermark sign (white arrow) in figure_1b; p0:tool:3 confirms all findings are on the right side. Option A matches this: wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity and engorged descending pulmonary artery both on the right. Option C lacks the wedge opacity, which is explicitly indicated.

observations.value: White arrow in image_2 points to a wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity labeled as Hampton's hump.

observations.attribute: Engorgement of descending pulmonary artery (Fleischner sign)
observations.value: Blue arrow in image_2 points to enlarged pulmonary artery (Fleischner sign); observation_4 confirms findings on right side, consistent with both X and Y mentioning right descending pulmonary artery engorgement.
White arrow in image_2 also labeled as Westermark sign (focal peripheral hyperlucency), which appears in Y but not X.

Observation_3 explicitly identifies all three signs (Hampton’s hump, Fleischner, Westermark) in image_2; however, X includes Hampton’s hump + Fleischner, while Y includes Fleischner + Westermark. The question asks for the combination *most suggestive* of PE. Hampton’s hump is more specific for acute PE than Westermark sign (which can be subtle or mimicked). Both signs are present, but X pairs the highly specific Hampton’s hump with Fleischner sign, whereas Y omits Hampton’s hump. Clinical literature favors Hampton’s hump + enlarged PA as a stronger indicator when both are present.

selector.followup_question: Is the wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton's hump) clearly demarcated, pleural-based, and associated with adjacent vascular pruning?

observations.value: White arrow in image_2 (observation_3) is labeled as Westermark sign; observation_4 confirms findings on the right side, consistent with Y's 'focal peripheral hyperlucency in the right lung field'.

Blue arrow in image_2 (observation_3) is labeled as Fleischner sign; both X and Y include 'engorgement of the right descending pulmonary artery', and observation_4 confirms right-side involvement. So this sign supports both equally.

Observation_3 labels a region as Hampton’s hump (white arrow at (40,54)-(46,60)), but followup_observation_1 (and its crop followup_image_1) states the opacity is faint, ill-defined, not clearly wedge-shaped or pleural-based, and lacks adjacent vascular pruning—i.e., not classic Hampton’s hump. Thus, the presence of a definitive Hampton’s hump is unsupported; this undermines X, which requires it.
Both X and Y specify right lung; observation_4 confirms all signs are on the right side.

The full original images (image_1–image_3) do not show a classic, clearly demarcated Hampton’s hump with associated vascular pruning.

observations.attribute: wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity in right lower lung field
observations.value: Blind observation confirms Hampton’s hump (triangular pleural-based opacity with base at diaphragm, apex toward hilum) in right lower zone; image_2 arrows point to this region (blue arrow at (33,50)-(40,56) and white arrow at (38,40)-(45,46) localize the area).

observations.attribute: engorgement of the right descending pulmonary artery
observations.value: Expert tool identifies Fleischner sign (enlarged pulmonary artery) at (38,40)-(45,46) in image_2; blind observer notes Palla’s sign as unresolved. However, image_3 expert analysis confirms findings are on the right side, and the arrow localization in image_2 is consistent with right descending PA. Neither X nor Y uniquely specifies laterality beyond 'right', so both share this support.
Blind observation and expert tool both identify Westermark sign (focal oligemia/hyperlucency) in right lower lobe (arrow at (33,50)-(40,56)), supporting Y’s inclusion of this sign.

Hampton’s hump + Fleischner sign together are more specific for acute PE than Westermark + Fleischner; blind report confirms both Hampton’s hump and Westermark are present, but X includes the classic triad component (Hampton’s hump) that is rarer and more diagnostic. Y omits Hampton’s hump, which is explicitly observed.

selector.followup_question: Is the wedge-shaped opacity truly pleural-based with a sharp pleural margin and no air bronchograms, distinguishing it from consolidation?

observations.attribute: pleural-based opacity in right lower lung zone
observations.value: present, wedge-shaped or triangular density abutting the pleura, with base at diaphragm and apex toward hilum (Hampton’s hump)
region of decreased pulmonary vascularity adjacent to the pleural opacity in right lower lung zone
cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (transverse diameter >50% thoracic width), though exact measurement not possible without scale
right hemidiaphragm appears higher than left; may be due to subpulmonic effusion or phrenic nerve involvement, but no clear costophrenic angle blunting
focal area of reduced vascularity in right lower lobe, distal to a region of increased vascularity (possible pruning), consistent with oligemic zone distal to embolus
not clearly visible; main pulmonary artery segment not definitively enlarged on available views
no overt meniscus or blunting of costophrenic angles; subtle density at right base may represent atelectasis or small effusion, but not definitive

uncertainties: Anatomical laterality (R/L) is marked but image orientation (PA vs AP, supine vs upright) is unresolved, affecting interpretation of diaphragmatic position and cardiac size.
No clinical context or comparison studies provided; cannot assess change over time.
Image resolution limits precise assessment of vascular pruning or subtle parenchymal changes.
Arrow annotations in image_2 indicate regions of interest but do not confirm diagnosis; their significance is interpretive, not intrinsic to the raw image.

choices.X: Wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity in the right lower lung field and engorgement of the right descending pulmonary artery
choices.Y: Engorgement of the right descending pulmonary artery and a focal peripheral hyperlucency in the right lung field
